flawed_step: Step 1 fails: going from 'no single-vertex move strictly increases the cut' to 'the cut is globally maximum'. Local optimality only means each vertex has at least as many neighbours on the other side as on its own side. That condition does not give global optimality: a vertex with equally many neighbours on each side can have a zero-gain move, and moving several vertices together can still raise the cut.
counterexample: G = C4 with vertices 1,2,3,4 and edges 12, 23, 34, 41. Partition A={1,2}, B={3,4}. Cut edges are 23 and 41, so the cut value is 2. Single moves: moving 1 gives {2} | {1,3,4}, with cut edges 12 and 23, so the value is 2. Moving 2 gives {1} | {2,3,4}, with cut edges 12 and 41, so the value is 2. Moving 3 gives {1,2,3} | {4}, with cut edges 34 and 41, so the value is 2. Moving 4 gives {1,2,4} | {3}, with cut edges 23 and 34, so the value is 2. No move strictly increases the cut, so the partition cannot be improved. But the partition {1,3} | {2,4} cuts all 4 edges, so its value is 4 > 2. The first partition is not a maximum cut.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The C4 counterexample was checked by hand. Every vertex has degree 2, with one neighbour on each side under {1,2}|{3,4}. So every single-vertex move leaves the cut value at 2, and the partition cannot be improved. The maximum cut, from the bipartition {1,3}|{2,4}, has value 4. What is actually true is a weaker bound: a partition that can't be improved by single moves cuts at least |E|/2 edges.
